*Nominated for Best Book at the 2025 Chortle Awards*

'Outstanding, I want to press it into the hands of every newly diagnosed person' Fern Brady

'Like a Martian's guide to living on Earth. Funny, enlightening and gobsmacking' Frank Skinner

'A hilarious, crystal-clear guide to autism' Phil Wang

'An illuminating and joyously entertaining book' Daily Express


Why were the other kids at school obsessed with Britney Spears instead of The Goon Show?
Why don't people ever say what they mean?
And... Why is everyone chewing so loudly?

Comedian Pierre Novellie was on stage when a heckler suggested he was autistic. Usually, this disruption would be water off a duck's back but two things made this heckler different: first, he was himself autistic. Second, he turned out to be absolutely right.

This random encounter led to a diagnosis of autism at the age of 31 that unravelled his world, explained his struggles and answered questions that had bothered him for his entire life.

At once a hilarious and insightful journey through autism and neurodivergence, an entertaining explainer for the uninitiated and observational comedy for the neurodiverse, this is the perfect read for anyone who has ever asked themselves: why can't I just enjoy things?

Book Description

A memoir by comedian Pierre Novellie exploring his late diagnosis of Autism Spectrum Disorder, providing a light-hearted and accessible examination of neurodiversity through the lens of observational comedy.

About the Author

Pierre Novellie is a stand-up comedian, writer, radio host and podcaster. He is co-host of The Frank Skinner Show on Absolute Radio, and the co-host of the hit Budpod podcast alongside Phil Wang. His TV appearances include World's Most Dangerous Roads (Dave), The Mash Report (BBC2), and Stand Up Central (Comedy Central).

On the radio, Pierre has performed on The Now Show (Radio 4) and hosted the BBC Sounds podcast series Obsessed With... SAS: Rogue Heroes. As a writer, Pierre was one of the regular writers on the rebooted Spitting Image (ITV/Britbox) and has also written on shows including Mock the Week (BBC2), The News Quiz (Radio 4) and The Mash Report (BBC2).

Pierre has performed stand-up around the world, including sell-out runs at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, residencies in Soho and nationwide tours.

Amazon Customer
5 out of 5 stars
Side effects may include chuckling to yourself in public
A funny, moving, and insightful look at autism through a comedian's lens. Once I started the book I wanted to devour it whole! Pierre's personal and professional experience make this a compelling read. Treating a (very) complex topic with care, Pierre explains the key issues without it becoming overwhelming. (The book furnishes with references the perhaps numerous readers who may crave more details.) For me, the book prompted a series of a-ha moments and a certain amount of self-knowledge may well be an unavoidable side-effect for neurodivergent and neurotypical readers alike. I started reading this book on a bus and I suspect that my uncontrollable laughter, much as I strove to contain it, may have caused my fellow passengers a vague sense of unease. Bear this in mind when selecting your reading location(s).

  • TwoCentsWorth
    5.0 out of 5 stars Hilarious, affirming, and insightful
    Reviewed in the United States on 1 April 2025
    Format: Kindle EditionVerified Purchase
    I'm a 70-year-old autistic woman who was diagnosed late in life. I instinctively learned at an early age to "mask," but as anyone who does this will tell you, it's exhausting and inflicts a high toll to deny who you are, day in and day out, without knowing you're doing it.

    Childhood trauma and moving every three years compounded the loneliness and bullying and led to a daily mantra of "Let me sleep; let me rest; let me die," which the diagnosis and getting out of the regular workforce (I started my own business working from home) finally eradicated and allowed me to heal.

    I don't know if non-autistics find this book funny, with probably very little to relate to.

    I found it hilarious, affirming, and insightful. Plus, it's just nice to know there are people out there like me, in many, many ways, even if I never meet them. My mantra now is "Maladaptation to insanity is sanity" because I find so many neurotypicals to be lacking in logic and sanity and compassion and no longer have to question why I'm not like them -- or try to be like them.

    5.0 out of 5 stars Great read if you own and operate a human brain
    Reviewed in the United States on 1 August 2024
    Verified Purchase
    Whether or not you have ASD, this book is a great read. Cleanly, concisely, and hilariously written, WCIJET?:ACGtA is both very personal and highly relatable. It's thoroughly researched and honest about where the gaps lie in the current science around ASD, and consistently lays out a logical, ethical, and compassionate case for understanding and acceptance of both autistic and NT points of view. It's an amalgamation of pop-psychology, humor, and memoir that's tough to describe, but definitely an excellent read.

    The only downside here is that if you have literally any type of off-kilter brain thing going on, even if it's not ASD specifically, you are going to feel seen by this book in a way that will make you feel unnerved and grumpy. Especially if you're an adult pondering what exactly is up with you that makes you feel like such an alien all the time. People close to you will ask you "what's up? You seem quiet lately" and you will have to say "I'm reading a book by a stand-up comedian who describes himself as having a 'village executioner physique' which nevertheless is so insightful into the experience of adult neuro-atypicality that I have spent the last week analyzing every single thought I have and action that I take and now I feel like I'm a little creature piloting a meat-gundam through the world while recalibrating the controls, sorry about that"

    Five stars.
